sections.text: From Peking University and Google, CITransNet is a context-integrated transformer for auction design. It maximizes seller revenue while staying incentive-compatible, discovers asymmetric solutions, and generalizes to auction sizes it never saw during training.

A classic problem in auction theory is designing a mechanism that maximizes the seller's revenue while staying incentive-compatible. Myerson solved the single-item case in 1981, but the multi-item case remains open, and prior deep methods assume fixed or symmetric auctions.

Real auctions are richer. In e-commerce advertising, many bidders compete for many ad slots described by features, and every round has a different number of participants. We need an architecture that absorbs context and handles varying auction sizes.

The paper makes two contributions. It extends the RegretNet framework to the contextual setting and proves a sample-complexity bound. And it introduces CITransNet, permutation-equivariant over bids and contexts, not restricted to symmetric auctions, with a parameter count independent of auction scale.

CITransNet takes three inputs: the bidding profile, bidder-contexts, and item-contexts. It embeds contexts with bids into a representation per bidder-item pair, then passes it through transformer interaction layers that mix a global average with row and column transformers, staying permutation-equivariant. A final layer outputs allocations and payments, with zero-regret enforced during training.

They evaluate on nine synthetic settings. Three single-item cases, A through C, have known Myerson-optimal solutions as a sanity check. The other six, D through I, are multi-item auctions up to five bidders and ten items, the largest size in the auction-design literature.

Results come in two parts. On single-item settings, CITransNet nearly recovers Myerson's optimal revenue, 0.593 against 0.594, with regret below one thousandth, while context-blind baselines fall short. On the harder multi-item settings, it beats the Item-wise Myerson baseline in all six configurations, with gains reaching ten percent.

To isolate why it works, the authors replace the transformer layers with RegretNet's fully-connected and EquivariantNet's equivariant layers, giving CIRegretNet and CIEquivariantNet. Both still get context, yet earn less revenue everywhere, pinning the gain on the transformer layers. Removing context hurts even easy settings.

A few numbers capture the impact. On the single-item benchmark, CITransNet reaches 0.593 versus the optimal 0.594. In the three-bidder ten-item setting it earns 6.872 against Item-wise Myerson's 6.509, and one continuous-context margin nears ten percent. It wins all six multi-item settings.

The takeaway: context as a first-class input unlocks better learned auctions. CITransNet is near-optimal, asymmetric when needed, and incentive-compatible. Its size-independent parameter count lets one trained model transfer to auction sizes it never saw.
